name: Ajanta Caves
info: The Ajanta Caves are 30 rock-cut Buddhist monasteries and worship halls carved into a gorge wall in Maharashtra, India, in two phases from about the 2nd century BCE to about 480 CE, and hold the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting.

facts.made: Buddhist monks, patrons and artisans in two phases: the first possibly under the Satavahana dynasty or the Maurya Empire, the second under donors at the court of the Vakataka emperor Harishena (Harisena), including his minister Varahadeva and the sub-king Upendragupta
facts.form: 30 caves cut from flood basalt in a 75-metre wall of rock: viharas (monasteries) with square halls and cells, and chaitya-grihas (worship halls) with a stupa in an apse; murals in dry fresco, and rock-cut sculpture
facts.where: The northern wall of the U-shaped gorge of the River Waghur on the Deccan Plateau, in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra, India; copies of the paintings are held among others by the Victoria and Albert Museum
facts.known: Jataka scenes painted in Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17; the bodhisattvas Padmapani and Vajrapani in Cave 1; the oldest surviving ancient Indian murals in Caves 10 and 11; the stupa-fronted Buddha in Caves 19 and 26; Spink's disputed brief chronology; the tiger-hunting party of 1819

t: The caves were cut in two phases: a first group of about the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE, and a second, larger group in the 5th century CE, which Walter Spink dates to the years 460 to 480 and other scholars place over a longer span.

Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 form the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting, which mostly tells the Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives; the later caves were paid for by single patrons seeking merit.

The site was known to local people and to pilgrims long before 1819, and its murals have since been damaged by neglect, varnish and cleaning, while many 19th-century copies of them were lost in fires.
dyk: In 1819 a British officer scratched his name and the date over a painting of a bodhisattva in Cave 10; because he stood on a five-foot pile of rubble, the inscription now sits well above the eye level of an adult.
ev: The earliest caves were begun, and the oldest inscription at the site, in Cave 10, is dated by its Brahmi letters to about this time
The Chinese pilgrim Faxian recorded Buddhist pilgrims visiting the site
Work on new caves began in many places at once under Harishena's court, according to Spink
Harishena died, and major excavation soon ceased except at Cave 26
John Smith, guided by a local shepherd boy to Cave 10, brought the caves to the attention of the British
A fire at the Crystal Palace in London destroyed all but four of Robert Gill's 27 copies of the murals
The last Nizam of Hyderabad had Italian restorers work on the paintings and turned the site into a museum
The Ajanta Caves were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
The Ajanta Caves lie in the northern wall of the U-shaped gorge of the River Waghur on the Deccan Plateau. They are generally agreed to have been made in two distinct phases, the first during the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE and the second several centuries later. The earliest group is caves 9, 10, 12, 13 and 15A. According to Walter Spink these were made between 100 BCE and 100 CE, probably under the patronage of the Satavahana dynasty (230 BCE to 220 CE); other datings prefer the period of the Maurya Empire (300 to 100 BCE). These first caves were paid for by a number of different patrons seeking merit, and several inscriptions record the donation of particular portions of a single cave.

The second phase began in the 5th century and is attributed to the theistic Mahayana tradition of Buddhism. Spink argues that the site lay dormant until the mid-5th century, although the early caves stayed in use and the Chinese pilgrim Faxian recorded pilgrims there around 400 CE. The later caves were each commissioned as a complete unit by a single patron from among the local rulers or their court elites, again for merit in the Buddhist afterlife, as inscriptions such as those in Cave 17 state.
sections.content:
The caves are 30 rock-cut Buddhist monuments carved into a wall of rock 75 metres long, though 36 foundations have been identified, some added later with letters such as 15A; the numbering is a convenience and does not follow the order of building. Most are viharas, monasteries with a square hall, a cloister-like aisle on each side and small square cells for monks, which in the later period gained a shrine with a large Buddha at the rear. The other main type is the chaitya-griha, a worship hall divided into a nave and two aisles by a row of pillars, with a stupa in the apse that visitors walked around. Caves 9 and 10 are early halls; caves 19 and 26 are later ones, with a Buddha carved on the stupa's front.

The walls hold paintings and sculpture. The paintings predominantly narrate the Jataka tales, legends of the Buddha's previous births as an animal or a human. Cave 1 concentrates on lives in which he was a king, and the two best-known single painted figures are the bodhisattvas Padmapani and Vajrapani beside its shrine entrance. Cave 2 shows many noble and powerful women, and one of its frescos shows children at a school. Caves 16 and 17 add scenes from the Buddha's life and further Jatakas.
sections.making:
The caves are carved from flood basalt and granite of the Deccan Traps. The rock is layered and variable in quality, which forced the carvers to change their plans in places and later caused cracks and collapses, such as the lost portico of Cave 1. Excavation began with a narrow tunnel cut at roof level that was widened downwards and outwards, as the unfinished caves 21 to 24 and the abandoned Cave 28 show. The artists probably carved the rock and made the pillars, roofs and idols themselves, and sculpture and painting inside a cave went on in parallel.

The murals are in dry fresco, painted on a dry plaster surface rather than into wet plaster. Compositions spread in all directions from a central figure or group instead of running in horizontal bands. In the later caves the painters generally worked on finished areas while excavation continued elsewhere in the cave. Spink's account has the work abandoned in 478 after a brief busy period, which he gives as the reason for unpainted areas such as Cave 4 and the plastered but never painted shrine of Cave 17. Lapis lazuli, which Pia Brancaccio notes must have come from Afghanistan or Iran, was used for the figures of foreigners.
sections.reception:
Scholars read the paintings as a view of life between the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE, showing royalty, the elite, common people, monks and rishis, along with shops, festivals and performance. They contrast the renouncing monk with the sensual life of the materialistic. Many figures in Caves 1, 2 and 17 have foreign faces or dress, which Brancaccio takes as evidence of a prosperous society active in international trade. Spink and other scholars hold that colonial art historians misdated the so-called Persian Embassy Scene in Cave 1 to the 7th century, and read it as an incomplete 5th-century painting of a Jataka tale.

Nineteenth-century European responses were often critical. William Dalrymple writes that Orientalists lacking knowledge of the Jataka tales could not understand the subjects and projected their own assumptions onto them, and early Western observers found the luxurious, sensuous paintings out of place in a monastic setting. Richard Cohen, by contrast, writes that to the Indian and Buddhist mind the caves are the religious and the secular fused together. Spink calls the site's rapid transformation between 460 and 480 one of the most remarkable creative achievements in human history.
sections.survival:
The caves were not forgotten. Faxian recorded pilgrims around 400, the Chinese traveller Xuanzang described them in the 7th century, a Rashtrakuta inscription of the late 7th or early 8th century is the last at the site, and Abu al-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari mentions twenty-four rock-cut temples. Richard Cohen suggests they stayed in use without a stable Buddhist community. On 28 April 1819 John Smith, a British cavalry officer hunting tigers, was shown the entrance to Cave 10 by a local shepherd boy; the caves were well known to locals already. He had villagers cut back the jungle and scratched his name over a painting.

Neglect and some restoration damaged the work. In the early 1920s the last Nizam of Hyderabad, whose territory included the site, had the paintings restored by two Italian experts and opened a museum and a road, efforts that Cohen says were mismanaged and hastened decay; according to Spink and others, Griffiths's cheap varnish and recent cleaning by the Archaeological Survey of India also harmed the murals. Robert Gill's copies of 1844 to 1863 mostly burned in 1866, and over a hundred of John Griffiths's canvases burned in 1885. A landslide in 1956 led to the excavation of Cave 30, perhaps the oldest cave.
sections.legacy:
The paintings and the style they come from probably influenced painting in Tibet and Sri Lanka, and some influence has been suggested at the Kizil Caves of the Tarim Basin. In the 19th and early 20th centuries a series of copying projects followed: Gill, Griffiths and his students, Christiana Herringham and a group from the Calcutta School of Art including Nandalal Bose, and the Japanese artist Arai Kampo, whose tracings perished in the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake. The Victoria and Albert Museum still holds 166 surviving Gill and Griffiths paintings.

The rediscovery gave Indian artists examples from ancient India to follow. Nandalal Bose experimented with ancient techniques in forming his own style, and Abanindranath Tagore and Syed Thajudeen also drew on the paintings. The caves inspired Anna Pavlova's ballet Ajanta's Frescoes, which premiered at Covent Garden in 1923, and the opening poem of Muriel Rukeyser's collection Beast in View (1944). The Archaeological Survey of India is responsible for the site, which UNESCO listed in 1983. The dating of the second phase remains disputed between Spink's brief chronology and a longer one.

summary: The Ajanta Caves in Maharashtra are 30 Buddhist rock-cut monasteries and worship halls made in two phases, from about the 2nd century BCE and in the 5th century CE. Their murals of the Jataka tales are the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting, and the dating of the second phase is still debated.

notes: start -200 circa: the article says 'starting around the second century BCE'; Spink places the early caves 100 BCE to 100 CE, others at the Maurya period (300 to 100 BCE).

Second-phase dating is disputed: older accounts 400-650 CE, Spink 460-480, Khandalavala, Shastri, Deshpande and Bakker a longer chronology to the mid-6th century; the ASI keeps the traditional dating. All three are given.
Harishena's reign is given as 460 to 477 by Spink and as c. 475 to c. 500 in the Cave 16 section; I used Spink's and left the other out.
Cave 4's date differs (ASI 6th century, Spink about 463); not used in the text. Caves 12 and 13 are also dated differently by ASI, Spink, and Gupte and Mahajan; left out.
The article says Cave 10 inscription is Sanskrit in Brahmi and dated c. 2nd century BCE; used only as the date of the oldest inscription.
